extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for making and evaluating inductive inference and causal reasoning, and for using probability to measure the degree of support that observations give to general laws. Includes distinctions between kinds of induction, definitions of cause, and the role of hypotheses and deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference never passes beyond the premises
rubrics_metrics.description: In inductive as in deductive reasoning the conclusion never passes beyond the premises. Reasoning adds no more to the implicit contents of our knowledge than the arrangement of specimens in a museum adds to their number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inference unfolds the hidden meaning of our observations; it proceeds on the assumption that future and unperceived will be governed by the same conditions as past and perceived. Use the museum analogy: arrangement allows perception of similarity but does not create new facts. Be cautious that reasoning cannot create new experiential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of conditions is the ground of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of condition between events from which we argue and those to which we argue must always be the ground of inference; such similarity may relate to time, place, logical combination of events, or any conjunction of circumstances involving quality, time, and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify inductive problems by which similarity applies: coexistence of qualities (e.g., yellow, ductile metals with high specific gravity), time similarity (e.g., recurrent pendulum beats or comet returns), space relations (e.g., triangles on a circle diameter). Ensure the similarity invoked is the relevant kind for the inference being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of inductive aims (laws vs. particular prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: That process only can be called induction which gives general laws, and it is by the subsequent employment of deduction that we anticipate particular events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating induction (establishing general rules) with direct case-to-case prediction. Logic's task is to analyze whether inferences have been correctly drawn (conditions for correctness), not merely to describe habitual associations that lead to predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent hypotheses and test by deductive consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases of inductive inference we must invent hypotheses until we fall upon some hypothesis which yields deductive results in accordance with experience; such accordance renders the chosen hypothesis more or less probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat observed regularities as suggestions for hypotheses. Prefer hypotheses that produce deductive consequences which can be checked against observations; increase the hypothesis's probability when deduction and experience agree. This emphasizes hypothesis-generation plus deductive testing rather than unanalysed generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the theory of probability to measure degree of support
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth or untruth of a natural law, when carefully investigated, resolves itself into a high or low degree of probability. The amount of uncertainty corresponds to the probability that other objects than those examined may exist and falsify our inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When certainty is unattainable, quantify or at least acknowledge the degree of support observations give to a law. Use probabilistic reasoning to avoid over- or under-estimating knowledge; the theory of probability is needed to calibrate confidence in inductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite instances cannot prove universal laws without deductive or theoretical justification
rubrics_metrics.description: No finite number of instances can ever prove a general law, or give us certain knowledge of even one other instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples may suggest laws but do not establish them conclusively (examples: numbers ending in 5 are divisible by 5 is provable deductively; numbers ending in 7 are not necessarily prime despite examples). Seek deductive reasons, mathematical principles, or deeper theory to justify universality; beware of being misled by large but finite regularities (Babbage example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require representativeness of observations (adequacy of sample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement (of observations) allows us to perceive similarities and peculiarities and, on the assumption that the museum is an adequate representation of nature, it enables us to judge prevailing forms of natural objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider whether the observed cases are representative of the wider class. Do not infer general laws unless the sample reasonably represents the target population of cases; lack of representativeness increases the chance of falsification by unobserved instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'cause' as aggregate antecedents and treat causal knowledge as probabilistic
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause may be defined as the sum or aggregate of all such accidents, both in the agents and the patients, as concur in producing the effect; or 'the object or event which immediately precedes any change, and which existing again in similar circumstances will be always immediately followed by a similar change.' These definitions may be accepted with the qualification that our knowledge of causes in such a sense can be probable only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting causes, specify the antecedents (positive or negative conditions) believed to produce an effect. Recognize that knowledge of causes from finite experience is probabilistic, not certain; avoid treating knowledge of a cause as guaranteeing certainty about future events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fallacious use of 'cause' that implies certainty from finite experience
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat causes as invariable antecedents that grant certain knowledge of the future is mistaken; either a cause is not an invariable antecedent, or we can never gain certain knowledge of causes from finite experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the word 'cause' act as a philosophical spell that obscures uncertainty. Be aware of the dilemma that finite experience cannot give certain knowledge of future events even when we name antecedents 'causes.' Maintain epistemic humility about causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat absence or removal as legitimate causal conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only may a cause be an existent thing endowed with powers, but the very absence or removal of a thing may also be a cause (e.g., dryness as cause of mummies' preservation; excavation of valleys as cause of mountain elevation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include negative conditions (absence, removal) when enumerating antecedents. Causal analyses should consider both positive presences and absences as part of the causal aggregate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate the question of existence of a cause from the question of its kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct questions must not be confused: (1) Is there any cause for the event? (2) Of what kind is that cause? The existence of any cause (vs. the classification of its character) are separate inferential problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining an event, first clarify whether one is arguing that some antecedent condition existed at all (existence question) or attempting to identify its nature or properties (classification question). These require different kinds of evidence and inferential procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deductive verification of conjectured general laws when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to have no confidence in any law until we have treated it deductively, and have shown that from the conditions supposed the expected results must ensue (example: prove divisibility by 5 from rules of decimal numeration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After hypothesizing a general law from observation, attempt to derive it from established principles or mathematical reasoning. Use deduction to transform a plausible empirical generalization into a law supported by necessary relations when available.
